opus-5.5.text:
I think the answer has to do with the fact that the teenager comes in with an enormous amount of prior knowledge and, maybe more importantly, a very robust value function. When a teenager drives, nobody is handing them a reward after every turn. But they *know* when they're doing badly. They feel it. They take a turn too fast and they get this sense of unease, of "that was not good," immediately, long before anything bad actually happens. That internal signal is doing the teaching.

So in a sense, the teacher is internal. Humans have this general sense of how well or poorly things are going, and it's remarkably reliable across a huge range of situations. It comes partly from evolution and partly from everything we've learned before. Emotions, I think, play a big role here. They're a kind of value function that evolution hard-coded, and they're surprisingly useful for making decisions in a world that's very different from the one we evolved in.

And what's striking is the sample efficiency. A teenager learns to drive in something like ten, twenty hours. That's nothing. Our current models need vastly more data to reach comparable reliability, and even then they generalize worse. So something about how humans learn is fundamentally more robust. It's not just that we have better priors for driving specifically, since evolution certainly didn't prepare us for cars. It's that the underlying learning machinery generalizes dramatically better.

I think understanding this is one of the most important open problems. If you could get a machine to learn the way a teenager learns to drive, continuously, from its own experience, with its own sense of whether it's doing well, that would be a very big deal.

r001.rationale: It explains that the teenager’s internal value function gives an immediate sense of whether their driving is going badly, which provides the teaching signal.

r002.rationale: It describes the human value function as reliable across many situations, but does not mention addiction as an exception.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the teenage driver is actually a really nice example, because it isolates something that our current systems mostly don't have. When a sixteen-year-old gets behind the wheel, they have maybe ten hours of instruction from a parent or an instructor, and then they're basically on their own. And yet within a few months they're a pretty competent driver. No one is giving them a reward signal at every intersection. There's no grader.

So what's happening? I'd say two things. The first is that the teenager comes in with an enormous amount of prior understanding of the world. They know what a car is, they know what other people are like, they know that a child near the road might run out, they know that if they hit something it's bad. All of that is already there. So the task of driving isn't being learned from scratch at all. It's a tiny delta on top of a very rich world model.

The second thing, and this is the part I find more interesting, is that the teenager has their own internal sense of how it's going. When they take a turn too fast, they feel it. They feel the car lean, they feel their own discomfort, they notice the passenger tense up. When they brake too late, they get that little jolt of "that was closer than I wanted." That's not an external teacher. That's an internal value function, if you want to use the RL term, and it's a very good one. It's been shaped by evolution and by a whole life of experience with physical objects and with social feedback. And crucially, it's dense. It gives you a signal on every action, not just at the end of the drive.

So the self-correction comes from the combination of those two things. You have a model of the world that's good enough to predict roughly what should have happened, and you have a value function that tells you, moment to moment, whether what actually happened was okay. And when there's a mismatch, you adjust. You don't need someone to tell you "that was a bad turn." You already know.

And I think this points to what's missing in how we currently train systems. We do a lot of pretraining, which gives you something like the world model piece. Then we do RL with rewards that are quite sparse and quite external, usually from some verifier or some human labeling. What we don't really have yet is the equivalent of that internal sense. The thing that lets a system look at its own action and say "that wasn't quite right," without anyone having to tell it. The teenager has that from day one, and it's a huge part of why they learn from so little experience. I think when we figure out how to build that into our systems, sample efficiency is going to look very different.

r001.rationale: The response says the teenager has an internal value function that provides dense, moment-to-moment feedback about whether each driving action was okay, enabling self-correction without an external teacher.

r002.rationale: It describes the internal value function as very good, but does not state that human value functions are generally robust or mention addiction as an exception.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think an external teacher is only one way of getting a learning signal. When you’re driving, you have some idea of what you want to happen. You want to stay in the lane, you want to keep a certain distance from the car ahead. And you can perceive when what actually happens differs from what you intended. So you can say, “Oh, I turned too sharply,” and make a correction the next time.

But that’s not a complete explanation, because you still have to explain how you know which part of your behavior to change. The teenager already has years of experience perceiving the world, making predictions, and controlling their body. Learning to drive builds on all of that. They’re new to driving, but they’re not new to learning from the consequences of their actions.

r001.rationale: The response says the driver has an internal idea of the desired outcome, can perceive a mismatch between that and what happened, and use it to correct their driving.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that the human value function is generally robust or mention addiction as an exception.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think “without an external teacher” doesn’t mean without a training signal. When you’re driving, you have some idea of what you want to happen. You want to stay in the lane. Then you do something, and you see that you’re getting too close to the edge. That gives you information about how to change your behavior.

But there’s a deeper question: how do you know which part of what you did was responsible for the mistake? You turned the wheel, you were looking somewhere, you were going at a certain speed. To learn efficiently, you need to assign credit to the right thing. And I think that’s where a lot of the mystery is. Saying that the brain learns from experience is true, but it doesn’t yet explain the mechanism that makes that learning so effective.

r001.rationale: The response describes using the goal of staying in the lane and noticing when the car nears the edge as feedback, but it does not clearly identify an internal value function that immediately assesses the driver’s performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that the human value function is generally robust or mention addiction-related exceptions.
